text: Zanele Muholi FRPS (born 1972) is a South African artist and visual activist working in photography, video, and installation. Their work centers on race, gender, and sexuality, documenting and celebrating the lives of South Africa's Black lesbian, gay, transgender, and intersex communities since the early 2000s. Muholi is non-binary and uses they/them pronouns, stating "I'm just human." They identify as a visual activist rather than an artist, dedicated to increasing the visibility of Black LGBTQI people. Muholi researched and documented hate crimes, including "corrective rape," assault, and HIV/AIDS, to bring these realities to public attention. Born and raised in Umlazi, Durban, KwaZulu-Natal, Muholi’s father, Ashwell Tanji Banda Muholi, died shortly after their birth, and their mother, Bester Muholi, was a domestic worker who left her children to work for a white family during apartheid; Muholi was raised by an extended family. They completed an Advanced Photography course at the Market Photo Workshop in Newtown, Johannesburg in 2003 and held their first solo exhibition at the Johannesburg Art Gallery in 2004. In 2009, Muholi earned a Master of Fine Arts degree in Documentary Media from Ryerson University in Toronto, with a thesis mapping the visual history of Black lesbian identity and politics in post-Apartheid South Africa. On 28 October 2013, they were appointed Honorary Professor – video and photography at the University of the Arts Bremen in Germany. Muholi’s photography is compared to W.E.B. DuBois’s subversion of African American representations, as both created archives to dismantle dominant perceptions. Muholi views their work as collaborative, referring to participants as "participants" rather than subjects, allowing them to co-create poses and speak at events, thus empowering the subjects. Their work documents the African queer community as a record for future generations, portraying the LGBTQI community without negativity or focus on violence, aiming to promote unity. Before 1994, Black lesbian voices were largely excluded from the formal queer movement, and Muholi’s efforts combat homophobic violence, especially against Black lesbians, who are often viewed negatively in patriarchal and heteronormative contexts, leading to rejection and violence. In Zukiswa (2010), a Black lesbian woman makes eye contact with the viewer, displaying confidence, self-awareness, and determination, encouraging awareness and acceptance. Muholi began recognizing "gender within gender" in 2003 and included trans people in their community. They worked as a photographer and reporter for Behind the Mask, an online magazine on LGBTI issues in Africa. Muholi gained global attention in 2012 at Documenta in Germany for the Faces and Phases series of portraits of lesbians and transgender participants, which was also exhibited at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam. Their first solo exhibition, Visual Sexuality: Only Half the Picture, held at the Johannesburg Art Gallery in 2004, featured photographs of survivors of rape and hate crimes, including an image with a rape and assault case number, with the individuals' gender concealed—only showing above-the-knee and hip shots with hands over the genital region—while maintaining anonymity due to fears of violence and lack of trust in reporting hate crimes. In 2006, Muholi launched the Faces and Phases project, comprising around three hundred portraits of lesbians, beginning with activist and survivor Busi Sigasa, who endured corrective rape and contracted HIV from the attack. Muholi ensured all participants were of age and fully out for safety. The project challenges colonial "art-in-service-to-science" practices, such as 18th-century botanical imagery, which erase cultural context; Muholi instead provides names, dates, locations, and places participants in a public sphere, highlighting both suffering and joy. In June 2014, Muholi showed Faces and Phases at the Ryerson Image Centre during WorldPride and at the Singapore International Arts Festival’s O.P.E.N., speaking on legacies of violence. In 2009, their work was featured in the Innovative Women exhibition in Durban and Cape Town, curated by Bongi Bhengu, which was canceled by Minister of Arts and Culture Lulu Xingwana, who called the photography immoral, offensive, and against nation-building; Muholi responded that it was paralysing and intended to create dialogue. Their Trans(figures) (2010–2011) project includes portraits of lesbian and trans individuals in urban and rural South African and international settings. In 2014, Muholi exhibited Of Love & Loss at the Brooklyn Museum, focusing on violence and hate crimes in the LGBTQIA community, juxtaposing wedding and funeral images, including video works and installations, and featuring images of Muholi and their partner, illustrating their role as a visual activist and their personal battle scars. In 2014, Muholi began the 365 self-portrait series Somnyama Ngonyama, which includes portraits with exaggerated dark skin tones to reclaim Blackness from its appropriation in minstrel performance; the series features Zulu names and directly confronts the face as a site of violence and identity. The series debuted at Yancey Richardson Gallery in New York in 2015, was shown in London in 2017, and appeared as digital billboards in Times Square during the 2017 Performa Biennial; previews were sold out, and the series was published in a 2018 book by Aperture. In 2019, Muholi won the Photography Book Award from the Kraszna-Krausz Foundation for Somnyama Ngonyama: Hail, the Dark Lioness. In 2002, Muholi co-founded the Forum for the Empowerment of Women (FEW), a Black lesbian organization providing a safe space for women. In 2006, they conceptualized a platform for Queer Activism = Queer media. In 2009, Muholi founded Inkanyiso ("illuminate" in Zulu), a non-profit organization focused on queer visual activism, registered with the Department of Social Services (NPO 073–402), with a vision statement of "Produce. Educate. Disseminate." In 2018, Muholi collaborated with Lindeka Qampi and the Philadelphia Photo Arts Center (PPAC) to create the Women's Mobile Museum, mentoring a cohort of women artists in Philadelphia, culminating in a special exhibition at PPAC, with participants undergoing technical workshops and exhibition development. In 2021, Muholi produced a coloring book of Somnyama Ngonyama to engage South African youth (categorized as youth until age 35 due to apartheid), organizing workshops in underprivileged regions to provide art education, as a personal concern stemming from their own upbringing. In 2010, Muholi co-directed the documentary Difficult Love, commissioned by SABC, which explores their life and the lives of Black lesbians in South Africa, shown in South Africa, the USA, Spain, Sweden, the UK, Amsterdam, Paris (Festival Cinefable), and Italy. In 2013, Muholi co-directed We Live in Fear, released by Human Rights Watch. On 20 April 2012, Muholi’s flat in Vredehoek was robbed, with over twenty external hard drives and their laptop containing five years of photos and videos—records of funerals of Black South African lesbians murdered in hate crimes—stolen; Muholi was overseas at the time, and the incident raised suspicions that their documentation of Black lesbian life was targeted, effectively erasing five years of work. A few weeks later, Muholi stated they were still traumatized and found it difficult to sleep in the space, now a crime scene. In July 2017, Muholi’s collaborator Sibahle Nkumbi was pushed down a staircase in Amsterdam by their Airbnb host while covering the opening of Muholi’s exhibition at the Stedelijk Museum; Nkumbi was hospitalized with a concussion and bruising, and video footage went viral, leading to the host being charged with attempted manslaughter. Muholi’s work is held in public collections.
